title: "Data Viewer"
format: html
---

The **Data Viewer** is the central place to inspect **non-video data over time**.

If the Media Viewer answers "what is happening in this frame?", the Data Viewer answers
"what is happening across this timeline?"

## What the Data Viewer Is For

Use the Data Viewer to:

- inspect continuous signals and sparse labels on one shared timeline,
- verify timing alignment across data modalities,
- compare raw and transformed outputs,
- quality-check labels and model outputs before downstream analysis.

This widget is designed for temporal interpretation, not frame-by-frame spatial annotation.

## Data Types You Can View

The Data Viewer focuses on time-series modalities:

- **Analog Time Series**: continuous-valued signals over time,
- **Digital Event Series**: instantaneous timestamps,
- **Digital Interval Series**: start/end temporal windows.

These are shown in stacked lanes on a shared time axis so you can directly compare relationships
between continuous activity and discrete labels.

For broader type definitions, see [Data Types](../../concepts/data_types.qmd).

## Time Alignment and TimeFrame

All display behavior is grounded in each feature's **TimeFrame**.

- Different modalities may have very different native sampling rates.
- The Data Viewer displays them on a common temporal view.
- This makes cross-modal checks possible (for example analog signal dynamics vs event/interval labels).

When something "looks off", verify the assigned TimeFrame first.
See [TimeFrame](../../concepts/timeframe.qmd).

## How the Display Works

At a practical level:

- You choose series from the feature tree.
- Each selected series is rendered with its own display settings.
- The view follows the application's global time position.
- You zoom time and amplitude to move from session-scale context to event-scale detail.

Typical lane rendering:

- analog as line traces,
- events as glyph/tick markers,
- intervals as blocks spanning time windows.

## Common Workflow

1. Add the relevant analog, event, and interval keys.
2. Set visibility/colors/scaling so overlays are legible.
3. Navigate time and zoom into important windows.
4. Check whether event/interval labels match signal structure.
5. Iterate with Data Inspector or transforms, then re-validate here.

This loop is one of the fastest ways to catch synchronization mistakes and labeling drift.

## Why It Is Central for Non-Video Data

Most downstream analysis depends on temporal consistency:

- thresholded events should coincide with meaningful signal changes,
- grouped intervals should track expected behavioral epochs,
- transformed outputs should preserve interpretable timing.

The Data Viewer is where these assumptions are visually validated before export, ML, or scripting.

## Relationship to Other Widgets

- **Data Manager**: create keys, set type, assign TimeFrame.
- **Data Viewer**: temporal validation and comparison.
- **Data Inspector**: curation and detailed editing.
- **Media Viewer**: spatial/frame-based annotation.

See [Interacting with Your Data](../../concepts/interface_roles.qmd) for the full division of roles.

## Practical Tips

- Keep derived outputs as new keys so you can compare source vs result side-by-side.
- Use consistent naming for related analog/event/interval series.
- Re-check TimeFrame assignments when combining hardware streams.
- Validate in Data Viewer before final export or model training.
